policy_title: Introduce a Digital Bill of Rights and regulate AI
stated: Introduce a Digital Bill of Rights to establish UK standards for rule of law and democracy in digital spaces, ensuring independent regulation of social media, safeguarding elections, and giving the public control over data. Push for a precautionary regulatory approach to AI, aligning with European and global efforts.

source.quote: Elected Greens would push to establish the UK as a leading voice on standards for the rule of law and democracy in digital spaces with a Digital Bill of Rights to ensure independent regulation of social media providers. The Digital Bill of Rights will give the public greater control over their data, ensuring UK data protection is as strong as any other regulatory regime. Elected Greens will push for a precautionary regulatory approach to the harms and risk of AI. We would align the UK approach with our neighbours in Europe, UNESCO and global efforts to support a coordinated response to future risks of AI.

bearing_set.reason: A Digital Bill of Rights directly addresses civil liberties, privacy, free expression, equal treatment, democratic/voting rights, and due process in digital spaces — core O9 indicators.

Giving the public control over data improves privacy (a core O10 indicator); independent social media regulation creates a contested effect on freedom of expression — the mechanism is direct and the direction is genuinely disputed.

A precautionary regulatory approach to AI materially affects the pace and terms of AI adoption in the UK, with credible competing arguments about whether tighter regulation slows productivity gains or enables investment certainty — a real non-negligible effect on living standards and economic opportunity.

membership_note: Three fundamentals earn real verdicts: O9 (democratic rights in digital spaces and election protection), O10 (data privacy improved, free speech effects contested), and O13 (AI regulatory posture has material consequences for productivity and economic opportunity). O5 is touched on only incidentally — the policy does not primarily target cybercrime or national security posture. O15 (cohesion) is plausible but the mechanism is too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar independently of O9 and O10.
